kurals.tamil:
அறம்பொருள் இன்பம் உயிரச்சம் நான்கின்
திறந்தெரிந்து தேறப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aramporul inbam uyirachcham naankin
Thirandherindhu thaerap padum.
kurals.meaning: A person should be trusted with office only after being examined in four ways: how he behaves when tempted through virtue, through wealth, through pleasure, and through fear for his own life.
kurals.elementary: Before a coach makes someone team captain, she quietly watches: Do they play fair even when cheating would win? Do they share the snacks? Do they get distracted by fun and forget practice? Do they stay brave when things get scary? Only a kid who passes all four gets the armband.
kurals.university: The chapter title pairs தெரிதல் (examining, discerning) with தெளிதல் (arriving at clear confidence), and this opening couplet names the method: testing by the four ‘ways’ (திறம்) of அறம், பொருள், இன்பம் and உயிரச்சம். Parimelazhagar reads these as deliberate trials of the candidate’s mind, a reading made vivid by Solomon Pappaiah, who describes staged provocations on grounds of righteousness, money and a woman’s supposed affection, plus a feigned threat to life. This matches almost point for point Kautilya’s four upadhās (religious, monetary, love and fear allurements) in Arthaśāstra 1.10, and commentators have long noted the correspondence. Kalaignar instead turns the tests into positive qualities (firm in dharma, honest in money, not infatuated by pleasure, unafraid for one’s life). Both web sources give the couplet identically; the final verb தேறப்படும் (‘is to be trusted’) sets the key root தேறு that recurs through the chapter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Teachers have decided that, in accordance with ascertained purity, the king shall employ in corresponding works those ministers whose character has been tested under the three pursuits of life, religion, wealth and love, and under fear.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya describes secret tests in which agents tempt each minister with a religious pretext, money, a love intrigue, and fear; only those who refuse are counted pure.
hinduism.tie_back: This names the same four tests as the Kural: dharma, wealth, pleasure and fear.
hinduism._accuracy_note: A near-exact match in content and number of tests; the Kural is often read with this text in mind.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy that church officers must be tested first and appointed only if found blameless.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the order is fixed: prove first, then entrust.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on testing before appointment; Paul does not list the four specific trials.

islam.quote_or_event: “One of the women said, ‘O my father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and the trustworthy.’”
islam.explanation: The daughter of the old man of Midian recommends hiring Moses after seeing his strength and honest conduct firsthand at the well.
islam.tie_back: Trustworthiness observed in action is the basis for hiring, as the Kural requires.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of hiring on proven character; it has no formal four-part test.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Moreover thou shalt provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.”
judaism.explanation: Jethro advises Moses to choose officials by character: capable, God-fearing, truthful and resistant to bribes.
judaism.tie_back: Fear of God and hatred of unjust gain match the Kural’s tests of dharma and of wealth.
judaism._accuracy_note: Covers two of the four tests explicitly; pleasure and fear for one’s life are not mentioned.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It’s through living together that a person’s virtue may be known, and then only after a long period, not a short period; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive; by one who is discerning, not by one who is not discerning.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells King Pasenadi that virtue, purity, endurance and discernment are each revealed by a different test (living together, trading, adversity, discussion) and only over time.
buddhism.tie_back: A four-part examination of character, each in its own arena, closely matches the Kural’s method.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Also has four tests, though they are not the Kural’s exact four; the setting even involves a king and his spies.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Returning to Ithaca disguised as a beggar, Odysseus tests the swineherd Eumaeus, the maids, the suitors and even Penelope, watching how each behaves toward a powerless stranger before revealing himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus deliberately hides his identity so that everyone’s true loyalty and greed come out.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a staged test of character before trust is given, as the Kural asks.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Captures covert testing well; the tests are informal rather than the four categories of the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates proposes that future guardians be watched from youth and put through labours, pains and conflicts, then through fears and then enchantments of pleasure, like gold tried in the fire, and only those who come out pure are made rulers.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s scheme deliberately exposes candidates to fear and to pleasure to see whether their convictions hold.
philosophy.tie_back: Testing by fear and by pleasure before giving authority is the core of the Kural’s fourfold trial.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close in method and purpose; Plato’s list of trials differs slightly from the Kural’s four.

kurals.tamil:
குடிப்பிறந்து குற்றத்தின் நீங்கி வடுப்பரியும்
நாணுடையான் சுட்டே தெளிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kudippirandhu kutraththin neengi vaduppariyum
Naanudaiyaan sutte thelivu.
kurals.meaning: Place your confidence in someone from a good family, who is free of faults and has the sense of shame that dreads any stain on his name.
kurals.elementary: Think about who you would let hold the class pet over the weekend. You would pick the kid from a caring home, who does not break rules, and who would feel really bad if people thought they had been careless. Feeling embarrassed about doing wrong is actually a superpower that keeps people honest.
kurals.university: Three qualifications are stacked: birth in a good lineage (குடிப்பிறப்பு), freedom from faults (குற்றம்), and நாண், the moral shame that fears a வடு, literally a scar, meaning a stain on one’s reputation. சுட்டே தெளிவு means ‘confidence rests on the one so pointed out’. Varadarasan and Pappaiah read குடி as literal family background, while Kalaignar reverses the logic: one who is faultless and ashamed of wrongdoing is thereby shown to be truly ‘high-born’, a reading that plays down birth in favour of conduct. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the first phrase as removing the faults of one’s birth-group. Both sources agree on the text; the idea of நாண் as a guard against wrongdoing returns at length in chapter 102 (நாணுடைமை).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…gentleness; modesty; steady determination; vigor; forgiveness; fortitude; cleanliness; and freedom from envy and from the passion for honor – these transcendental qualities, O son of Bharata, belong to godly men endowed with divine nature.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the qualities of a divine nature, including hrī (modesty, shame at doing wrong), and calls such a person abhijāta, ‘well-born’.
hinduism.tie_back: Being well-born and having a sense of shame are paired as marks of a trustworthy nature, as in the Kural.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the pairing of noble birth and shame; the Gita is describing spiritual character rather than choosing officials.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Moreover he must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul requires that a church overseer be well regarded even by outsiders, so he does not bring disgrace.
christianity.tie_back: Concern for an unstained reputation matches the Kural’s ‘shame that dreads a stain’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on reputation and avoiding reproach; family lineage is not raised here.

islam.quote_or_event: “If you don’t feel ashamed (from Haya’: pious shyness from committing religeous indiscretions) do whatever you like.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet quotes an old prophetic saying: without ḥayāʾ (moral shame), nothing holds a person back.
islam.tie_back: The Kural trusts the man of நாண் for the same reason: shame is what keeps him from wrong.
islam._accuracy_note: Direct parallel on shame as a moral restraint; the saying is not about appointments. Spelling ‘religeous’ is as on the source.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that shame is a good sign in a person, since one who feels shame will not quickly come to sin, and it links a shamefaced disposition with descent from those who stood at Sinai.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic tradition treats bushah (shame) as a moral safeguard and even as a mark of good lineage.
judaism.tie_back: Lineage and shame as a guard against sin are the two anchors of this Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not quoted; the pairing of shame and ancestry is a strong conceptual match.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha calls hiri (conscience, shame at wrongdoing) and ottappa (concern for blame) the two bright qualities that guard the world; without them society would fall into confusion.
buddhism.explanation: These two qualities are what stop a person from doing wrong even when unobserved.
buddhism.tie_back: நாண் that fears a stain is almost exactly hiri joined with ottappa.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close conceptual match on shame; Buddhism does not stress family birth in the same way.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Protagoras’ myth, Zeus fears the human race will destroy itself and sends Hermes to give every person aidōs (shame, respect) and dikē (justice), ordering that anyone lacking them be put to death as a plague to the city.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes shame a precondition for anyone to take part in civic life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise makes shame a precondition for public trust.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on shame as civic qualification; says nothing of lineage or selecting officers.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In any office of trust or stewardship, on the other hand, the opposite rule should be observed; for more virtue than ordinary is required in the holder of such an office, but the necessary knowledge is of a sort which all men possess.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle names loyalty to the constitution, administrative capacity and virtue as the qualifications for high office, and says that posts of trust call above all for exceptional virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Aristotle makes character, not skill alone, the test of whom a ruler should trust.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Politics, Book V, ch. 9 (1309a–b) (tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett, Politics Book V, Part IX). Partial match: Aristotle shares the emphasis on virtue in those entrusted with office, but has nothing on good family or on the sense of shame (naan) that the Kural stresses.

kurals.tamil:
அரியகற்று ஆசற்றார் கண்ணும் தெரியுங்கால்
இன்மை அரிதே வெளிறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ariyakatru aasatraar kannum theriyungaal
Inmai aridhe veliru.
kurals.meaning: Even among people who have studied difficult works and seem free of flaws, close examination will rarely find one without some ignorance.
kurals.elementary: Even the smartest kid in class, the one who knows every dinosaur name, might not know how to tie their shoes. Nobody knows everything. So when you choose someone for a job, check carefully instead of assuming they are perfect.
kurals.university: The couplet tempers the previous two: even the learned (அரிய கற்று) and flawless (ஆசு அற்றார்) will, on examination (தெரியுங்கால்), rarely be found without வெளிறு. வெளிறு literally means ‘whiteness’ and is used of weak, pale timber, and commentators gloss it as அறியாமை (ignorance) or a hidden weak spot. The practical lesson is that selection is not a search for a perfect person but a realistic judgment, which sets up the weighing of strengths and faults in the next couplet (504). Varadarasan and Pappaiah stress that no one is wholly free of ignorance, while Kalaignar aims the point at reputation: even those praised as flawless cannot be assumed so without examination. The text is the same in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Every endeavor is covered by some fault, just as fire is covered by smoke.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that no action in the world is entirely free of defect, just as no fire burns without smoke.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural makes the same point about people: some flaw is always there if you look.
hinduism._accuracy_note: The Gita speaks of actions rather than persons, but the ‘no flawless case’ logic is the same.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body.”
christianity.explanation: James admits that everyone stumbles in many ways; only a hypothetical perfect man would not.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it expects some flaw even in the best.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good general parallel; James is speaking of moral stumbling rather than ignorance.

islam.quote_or_event: “We raise in degrees whom We will, but over every possessor of knowledge is one [more] knowing.”
islam.explanation: After Joseph outwits his brothers, the Qur’an notes that above every learned person there is someone who knows more.
islam.tie_back: No learned person has complete knowledge, which is the Kural’s point.
islam._accuracy_note: A close match on the limits of every scholar’s knowledge.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For there is not a righteous man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not.”
judaism.explanation: Koheleth observes that no one, however righteous, is wholly without fault.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same realism to choosing people.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in spirit; it concerns sin rather than ignorance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There never was, there never will be, nor is there now, a person who is wholly blamed or wholly praised.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that no person in any age is entirely praiseworthy or entirely blameworthy.
buddhism.tie_back: Even the best will have something to fault, as the Kural says.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close; the following verses (229-230) even speak of praise earned by observing someone day after day.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Thetis dips the infant Achilles in the river Styx to make him invulnerable, but the heel she holds stays dry, and he is later killed by an arrow there.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greatest of heroes still has one weak spot.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s வெளிறு is exactly this kind of hidden weak spot in someone who seems perfect.
greek_mythology.source: Statius, Achilleid 1 (the Styx dipping); the heel detail belongs to later tradition
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A vivid image of hidden weakness; the myth is about physical vulnerability rather than ignorance, and the heel is post-Homeric.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seeking to test the oracle that no one was wiser than he, Socrates questions politicians, poets and craftsmen with great reputations for wisdom, and finds each of them, on examination, ignorant of much they claimed to know.
philosophy.explanation: Close questioning shows that those with the highest reputations still lack real knowledge.
philosophy.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s ‘when examined’ (தெரியுங்கால்).
philosophy._accuracy_note: An excellent match; Socrates’ method is the examination the Kural describes.

kurals.tamil:
குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி அவற்றுள்
மிகைநாடி மிக்க கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kunamnaadik kutramum naadi avatrul
Migainaadi mikka kolal.
kurals.meaning: Look into a person’s virtues, then look into his faults, then see which of the two outweighs the other, and judge him by what prevails.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a friend who sometimes forgets your birthday but always shares, always helps, and always tells the truth. If you put the good things on one side of a see-saw and the forgetful thing on the other, the good side sinks way down. That’s how the Kural says to judge people: by which side is heavier.
kurals.university: The verb நாடு (to seek, look into) occurs three times, giving a three-step procedure: examine குணம் (good qualities), then குற்றம் (faults), then மிகை (which is greater), and finally கொளல், ‘take’ the person according to what is மிக்க (predominant). Following 503’s point that no one is flawless, this is a rule of proportion rather than perfection. Pappaiah narrows it to appointment (choose by the excess of virtues), while Kalaignar keeps it general: a clear judgment about someone comes only after this weighing. Some commentators note the ambiguity of மிக்க கொளல்: judge the person by what predominates, or keep the one in whom virtues predominate; either way the method is the same. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Sometimes the mode of goodness becomes prominent, defeating the modes of passion and ignorance, O son of Bharata. Sometimes the mode of passion defeats goodness and ignorance, and at other times ignorance defeats goodness and passion.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that everyone has all three guṇas, and a person’s character is known by which one is dominant.
hinduism.tie_back: Judging someone by the quality that prevails is the Kural’s rule of மிகை.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of judging by the dominant element in a mixed nature; it is a metaphysical teaching, not a hiring rule.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins.”
christianity.explanation: Peter teaches that great love outweighs and covers many faults.
christianity.tie_back: The idea that a strong virtue can outweigh faults is close to the Kural’s weighing.
christianity._accuracy_note: A partial parallel on virtue outweighing fault; Peter is urging love, not a method of assessment.

islam.quote_or_event: “Then as for one whose scales are heavy [with good deeds], … But as for one whose scales are light, …”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgment each person’s deeds are weighed; the fate of each depends on which side is heavier.
islam.tie_back: The Kural uses the same image of a balance: judge by which side tips.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong structural match on weighing good against bad; the Qur’an speaks of divine judgment, not human selection.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Everything is foreseen yet freedom of choice is granted, And the world is judged with goodness; And everything is in accordance with the preponderance of works.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Akiva teaches that judgment follows the preponderance of a person’s deeds.
judaism._accuracy_note: A close verbal and conceptual match; Maimonides (Hilkhot Teshuvah 3:1) develops the same weighing idea.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Salt Crystal discourse the Buddha explains that a small bad deed by someone of great, developed goodness is like a pinch of salt in the Ganges, while the same deed by someone with little goodness is like salt in a cup of water.
buddhism.explanation: The effect of a fault depends on how much good surrounds it.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise judges faults in proportion to a person’s virtues.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Captures proportion well; the sutta concerns karmic results rather than evaluating candidates.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Before Achilles and Hector fight, Zeus lifts his golden scales with the fates of both warriors; Hector’s side sinks toward Hades, and Apollo leaves him.
greek_mythology.explanation: The gods decide by weighing and seeing which side is heavier.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s method is a moral version of these scales.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The weighing image matches; what is weighed is fate, not virtue and fault.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says that someone who strays only a little from the right, whether toward excess or deficiency, is not blamed; only the one who strays far is, and how far is a matter for perception in particular cases.
philosophy.explanation: Moral judgment of a person allows for small deviations and looks at the overall pattern.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural too tolerates lesser faults when virtues clearly prevail.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a reasonable parallel on proportionate judgment, not a direct weighing of virtues against faults.

kurals.tamil:
பெருமைக்கும் ஏனைச் சிறுமைக்கும் தத்தம்
கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Perumaikkum aenaich chirumaikkum thaththam
Karumame kattalaik kal.
kurals.meaning: For greatness and for its opposite, meanness, each person’s own deeds are the touchstone.
kurals.elementary: A jeweller checks whether a ring is real gold by rubbing it on a special black stone and looking at the streak. You can check whether someone is really kind the same way, by looking at what they actually do, not what they say or what they wear.
kurals.university: கட்டளைக் கல் is the goldsmith’s touchstone (உரைகல்): gold rubbed on it leaves a streak whose colour shows its purity. The couplet says that deeds (கருமம், from Sanskrit karma) are such a stone for both பெருமை (greatness) and சிறுமை (meanness), and the emphatic ஏ in கருமமே excludes other tests such as birth, wealth or eloquence. It completes the lesson of 502: family is a starting presumption, but conduct is the decisive proof. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads கட்டளைக் கல் as an inscribed ‘edict stone’ that guides conduct, but the touchstone reading of Varadarasan, Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Pope (‘touchstone true’) is standard. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…theoretical and practical knowledge, foresight, retentive memory, and affability shall be tested from successful application in works…”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya lists how each quality of a candidate minister is to be verified, and ability is judged by work actually done.
hinduism.tie_back: Work as proof of worth is the Kural’s touchstone.
hinduism._accuracy_note: A direct match for the selection setting; Kautilya also uses other tests (reliable witnesses, association) for other qualities.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says people are known by what their lives produce, as trees are known by their fruit.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Fruits’ play the role of the Kural’s touchstone of deeds.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says that tribes and peoples exist so we may know one another, but true nobility is measured by righteousness.
islam.tie_back: Greatness is measured by conduct, not lineage, as the Kural says.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on nobility through conduct; the Qur’an speaks of righteousness before God rather than observed deeds as evidence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Study is not the most important thing, but actions; whoever indulges in too many words brings about sin.”
judaism.explanation: Shimon ben Gamaliel teaches that deeds, not learning or talk, are what finally count.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too treats action as the decisive test.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on the primacy of deeds; it is about religious practice rather than assessing others.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by birth is one an outcast; not by birth is one a brahman. By deed one becomes an outcast, by deed one becomes a brahman.”
buddhism.explanation: Insulted as an ‘outcast’, the Buddha replies that high and low status come from conduct, not birth.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim that deeds are the touchstone of greatness and meanness.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipāta 1.7, Vasala Sutta, v. 21 (trans. Piyadassi Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: An almost exact parallel covering both greatness and lowness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Instead of taking the safe sea route, the young Theseus walks the bandit-infested road to Athens, defeating Periphetes, Sinis, Sciron and Procrustes, so that his deeds announce him before his father Aegeus recognises him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Theseus proves he is worthy of his royal birth by what he does on the road.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His deeds, not his birth tokens alone, are the touchstone of his greatness.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A reasonable narrative illustration; it concerns proving heroism rather than evaluating someone for office.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave acts, so that character is formed and shown in activity.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, virtue is a settled disposition revealed by repeated action.
philosophy.tie_back: If character shows itself in action, then deeds are the fair touchstone the Kural names.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; Aristotle stresses how character is formed rather than how others should assess it.

kurals.tamil:
அற்றாரைத் தேறுதல் ஓம்புக மற்றவர்
பற்றிலர் நாணார் பழி.
kurals.transliteration:
Atraaraith thaerudhal ombuga matravar
Patrilar naanaar pazhi.
kurals.meaning: Avoid placing trust in those who have no ties of kin or community, for having no attachments they feel no shame at disgrace.
kurals.elementary: Why do people usually behave well? Partly because they don’t want to let down their family, friends and neighbours. Someone who doesn’t care about anyone might not care if they get in trouble either. So the Kural says: be careful before trusting someone who has no one they care about.
kurals.university: அற்றார் means ‘those who are cut off’; the standard commentary (followed by Varadarasan, Pappaiah and Pope) takes it as those without kin (சுற்றம்), who are therefore பற்றிலர், without attachments, and so நாணார் பழி, unashamed of blame. The reasoning links back to 502: shame works through the people whose opinion one values, so someone with no such bonds has no brake. Kalaignar reads அற்றார் as the unprincipled (நெறியற்றவர்), and Sivayogi Sivakumar reverses the sense, reading it as a call to raise up those who have nothing, a reading at odds with the chapter’s context. ஓம்புக here means ‘guard against, avoid’. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Let him appoint seven or eight ministers whose ancestors have been royal servants, who are versed in the sciences, heroes skilled in the use of weapons and descended from (noble) families and who have been tried.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king to choose ministers with deep hereditary ties to the court and to noble families, and who have been tested.
hinduism.tie_back: Ministers rooted in family and loyalty are the opposite of the unattached people the Kural warns against.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Positive version of the same rule; it does not give the Kural’s reason (that the unattached feel no shame).

christianity.quote_or_event: “One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity; (For if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?)”
christianity.explanation: Paul makes a man’s care for his own household a qualification for leading the church.
christianity.tie_back: Family bonds, well kept, show the kind of person who can be trusted with more.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that household ties bear on fitness for office; the reasoning is about competence rather than shame.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that the best of people are those who are best to their families, adding that he was the best of them to his own family.
islam.explanation: A person’s treatment of kin is presented as a measure of goodness.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise reads a person’s bonds with kin as evidence of trustworthiness.
islam._accuracy_note: Only a loose parallel: it values family ties but does not warn against trusting the unattached.

judaism.quote_or_event: “…one from among thy brethren shalt thou set king over thee; thou mayest not put a foreigner over thee, who is not thy brother.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah requires Israel’s king to be one of their own kin, bound to the people he rules.
judaism.tie_back: Authority goes to someone with ties to the community, as the Kural advises.
judaism._accuracy_note: About kinship with the nation rather than personal family ties; it gives no shame-based reason.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Rhinoceros Horn discourse the Buddha praises the renunciant who drops all ties of children, wife, parents, wealth and kin and wanders alone like a rhinoceros horn.
buddhism.explanation: For the seeker of liberation, freedom from attachment is an ideal, not a danger.
buddhism.tie_back: This is a contrast: the Kural is speaking of state service, where the unattached lack the social brake of shame.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Deliberately a contrast rather than a parallel; the two texts value non-attachment differently because their goals differ.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Nestor warns the Achaean chiefs that a man who loves the horror of civil strife is clanless, lawless and hearthless (aphrētōr, athemistos, anestios).
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer groups being without clan, without law and without hearth as the marks of a dangerous man.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Being without kin and without restraint go together, just as the Kural says.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A strong parallel linking lack of kin with lack of restraint; paraphrased from the Greek.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that man is by nature a political animal, and that one who is by nature without a city is either a bad man or above humanity, like the ‘tribeless, lawless, hearthless one’ Homer condemns.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, ties to household and city are what make ethical life possible.
philosophy.tie_back: The rootless person, lacking these ties, is the one the Kural warns us not to trust.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; very close in reasoning, though Aristotle speaks of the city rather than of kin specifically.

kurals.tamil:
காதன்மை கந்தா அறிவறியார்த் தேறுதல்
பேதைமை எல்லாந் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaadhanmai kandhaa arivariyaarth thaerudhal
Paedhaimai ellaan tharum.
kurals.meaning: To trust people who lack the knowledge they need, merely because you are fond of them, brings every kind of folly.
kurals.elementary: Your best friend is awesome, but if they’ve never baked anything, you wouldn’t make them in charge of the cake for the whole school fair just because you like them. Liking someone is not the same as them being good at the job.
kurals.university: காதன்மை கந்தா means ‘with affection as the post’: கந்து is the post or pillar to which something is tied, so affection becomes the only support of the choice. அறிவு அறியார், ‘those who do not know what should be known’, names the risk, and the result is பேதைமை எல்லாம், every kind of folly. Pappaiah reads it as the folly produced by favouritism in appointments, and Kalaignar adds that such choices bear only useless results. Varadarasan’s printed gloss says the chooser’s ‘ignorance will perish’, which appears to be a typographical slip given his other readings and Pope’s ‘the height of folly’. The text reads எல்லாந் தரும் (sandhi of எல்லாம் + தரும்) in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The blind king Dhritarashtra, out of love for his son Duryodhana, repeatedly sets aside the counsel of Vidura and Bhishma and lets Duryodhana and his companions direct the kingdom, leading to the ruinous Kurukshetra war.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata presents Dhritarashtra’s affection as the root of the Kuru downfall.
hinduism.tie_back: Trusting an unwise person out of love brings ‘every folly’, as the Kural warns.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Vidura’s counsels and Dhritarashtra’s responses)
hinduism._accuracy_note: An exemplary narrative match; summarized rather than quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons.”
christianity.explanation: James forbids partiality, favouring some people for reasons other than merit.
christianity.tie_back: Favouritism is the trap the Kural names.
christianity._accuracy_note: Warns against partiality generally (James’ example is favouring the rich) rather than appointing the incompetent out of affection.

islam.quote_or_event: “When honesty is lost, then wait for the Hour (Doomsday).” The Bedouin said, “How will that be lost?” The Prophet (ﷺ) said, “When the power or authority comes in the hands of unfit persons, then wait for the Hour (Doomsday.)”
islam.explanation: Giving authority to people unfit for it is described as a betrayal of trust and a sign of the end times.
islam.tie_back: Entrusting affairs to the unqualified is the ‘folly’ the Kural warns of.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on the danger of unfit appointees; affection as the cause is not mentioned.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But he forsook the counsel of the old men which they had given him, and took counsel with the young men that were grown up with him, that stood before him.”
judaism.explanation: Rehoboam rejects experienced advisers in favour of the friends he grew up with, and their harsh advice splits the kingdom of Israel.
judaism.tie_back: Trusting familiar friends over the wise is exactly the folly the Kural describes.
judaism._accuracy_note: A very close narrative match: fondness and familiarity over competence, with ruinous results.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should a seeker not find a companion who is better or equal, let him resolutely pursue a solitary course; there is no fellowship with the fool.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha advises going alone rather than attaching oneself to a fool.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural similarly warns against binding oneself to the unwise, however dear.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on avoiding the unwise; affection as the motive is not addressed.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Having sworn by the Styx to grant his son Phaethon any wish, the loving sun-god Helios lets the untrained boy drive the chariot of the Sun; Phaethon loses control, scorches the earth, and is struck down by Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: A father’s love leads him to hand a great task to someone without the skill for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Affection as the only ‘post’ of trust ends in disaster, just as the Kural predicts.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Nearly a perfect illustration; the story is Roman in telling but Greek in origin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli writes that the choice of ministers is of no small importance to a prince, and that the first opinion people form of a ruler’s intelligence comes from the men he keeps around him.
philosophy.explanation: A ruler is judged by the quality of those he appoints.
philosophy.tie_back: Choosing incompetent favourites exposes the chooser’s own folly, which is the Kural’s point.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong on the consequences of appointments, less explicit about affection as the cause.

kurals.tamil:
தேரான் பிறனைத் தெளிந்தான் வழிமுறை
தீரா இடும்பை தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thaeraan piranaith thelindhaan vazhimurai
Theeraa idumbai tharum.
kurals.meaning: Whoever puts confidence in a stranger without examining him brings endless sorrow, even on his descendants.
kurals.elementary: If a stranger at the park says, “Give me your house key and I’ll water your plants,” and you just hand it over, trouble could follow your whole family for a long time. Trust has to be earned before you give it.
kurals.university: தேரான் (‘without examining’) and பிறன் (‘another, an outsider’) define the fault, and தெளிந்தான் (‘he who trusted’) the one who commits it. The key phrase வழிமுறை is read by Varadarasan and Kalaignar as ‘those who come after him’, his descendants, so the harm outlives the one who made the mistake; Pope follows this (‘on all his race’). Pappaiah shifts பிறன் to someone indifferent to the nation’s interests, a modern political reading. The second line தீரா இடும்பை தரும் is repeated word for word in 510, framing the chapter’s last three couplets with the same warning. ytamizh prints the couplet without the final full stop; the words are otherwise identical in both sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Queen Kaikeyi trusts the counsel of her maid Manthara without examining her motives, demands Rama’s exile and Bharata’s coronation, and so brings grief on Dasharatha, who dies, and on the whole royal house.
hinduism.explanation: One unexamined confidence sets off suffering for a whole dynasty.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural warns that unexamined trust brings sorrow that passes down to one’s line.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Manthara is a long-time servant rather than a stranger, but the lasting family harm of unexamined trust fits well.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that people who look harmless may be dangerous inside, so appearances must be tested.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural too warns against trusting an unexamined outsider on appearances.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on the danger of untested trust; harm to descendants is not mentioned.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful.”
islam.explanation: Believers are told to check reports from untrustworthy people before acting on them.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s rule is the same: investigate first or face lasting regret.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on investigating before trusting; it concerns news and reports rather than choosing people.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the men took of their provision, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Gibeonites pretend to be travellers from far away; Joshua’s leaders make a sworn treaty without proper inquiry, and that oath binds Israel for generations, returning as a famine in David’s time (2 Samuel 21).
judaism.tie_back: An unexamined agreement with strangers brings trouble on later generations, which is the Kural’s வழிமுறை.
judaism._accuracy_note: An excellent match on strangers, lack of scrutiny and consequences for descendants.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by appearance is a man rightly known, nor should trust be based on a quick glance, — for, disguised as well-restrained, the unrestrained go through this world.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha warns King Pasenadi that people who look disciplined may not be, so trust must not be given at a glance.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s தேரான் தெளிவு: trust without examination.
buddhism.source: Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.11, verse (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, as given in notes to Udāna 6.2)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close on not trusting at a glance; lasting harm to one’s line is not mentioned.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Trojans take in Sinon, a Greek stranger with a convincing story, believe him without proper testing, and drag the wooden horse into the city, leading to the fall of Troy and the end of Priam’s line.
greek_mythology.explanation: Laocoön’s warning is ignored and one act of unexamined trust destroys a whole city and dynasty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Trusting an untested stranger brings sorrow that does not end, just as the Kural says.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A near-perfect narrative match; the telling is Virgil’s Latin epic of a Greek myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero, following Theophrastus, says one should love after judging, not judge after loving, and notes that people who make friends hastily often come to regret it.
philosophy.explanation: Judgment must come before attachment, or regret follows.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural states the same order and the same cost of reversing it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a close conceptual match about friendship rather than appointments.

kurals.tamil:
தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது தேர்ந்தபின்
தேறுக தேறும் பொருள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thaerarka yaaraiyum thaeraadhu thaerndhapin
Thaeruga thaerum porul.
kurals.meaning: Trust no one without examining him; once you have examined him, trust him in the matters in which he can be trusted.
kurals.elementary: Before you lend your favourite bike, you watch how your cousin treats their own toys. Once you’ve seen they’re careful, you lend it without nagging them every five minutes. Check first, then really trust.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on two nearly identical roots: தேர் (to examine, choose) and தேறு (to trust, be confident). Almost every word is built on them, a characteristic Valluvar wordplay that makes the rule easy to remember: தேறற்க … தேராது (do not trust without examining), தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக (after examining, trust). The closing phrase தேறும் பொருள் is read in two ways: Varadarasan and Kalaignar take it as trusting in what deserves trust, while the older commentary followed by Pope takes it as entrusting to each person the duties suited to what the test showed. Pappaiah adds the practical corollary that one should not doubt someone after appointing them, which leads into 510. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Of these tried ministers, those whose character has been tested under religious allurements shall be employed in civil and criminal courts…”
hinduism.explanation: After the four tests, Kautilya assigns each minister to the kind of work his proven integrity suits.
hinduism.tie_back: Examine first, then entrust the matters the person has proved fit for, as the Kural’s தேறும் பொருள் suggests.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches both halves of the couplet as the older commentary reads it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay hands suddenly on no man, neither be partaker of other men’s sins: keep thyself pure.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns Timothy not to ordain anyone hastily, since he shares responsibility for their faults.
christianity.tie_back: This is the first half of the Kural: trust no one without examination.
christianity._accuracy_note: A strong match for the warning against haste; the second half (then trust fully) is not stated.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due and when you judge between people to judge with justice.”
islam.explanation: Trusts, including offices, must be given to those who are properly qualified for them.
islam.tie_back: Giving each trust to its rightful holder is the Kural’s ‘trust him in what he can be trusted with’.
islam._accuracy_note: Good on matching trusts to the right people; the testing step is implied rather than stated.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Sira advises that if you want a friend you should acquire him through testing and not be quick to trust him, since some are friends only when it suits them.
judaism.explanation: The Jewish sage makes testing the doorway to trust.
judaism.tie_back: The same sequence as the Kural: test, then trust.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a close match. Ben Sira is outside the Hebrew canon but was widely quoted in rabbinic literature.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells the Kalamas not to accept teachings on report, tradition or a teacher’s authority, but when they know for themselves, after examination, that something is skilful and leads to welfare, then to take it up and live by it.
buddhism.explanation: Acceptance is to follow personal examination, and once examined it is to be acted on fully.
buddhism.tie_back: The same two-step: examine, then commit.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Structurally close; it concerns accepting teachings rather than trusting people.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable, a man buying an ass takes it home on trial and turns it loose among his herd; it goes straight to the laziest, greediest animal, so he returns it, saying he can already tell what it is from the company it chose.
greek_mythology.explanation: The buyer tests before committing, and the test reveals the animal’s character.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Examine before you trust, as the Kural’s first line commands.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Ass and His Purchaser’
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates testing before commitment; the fable shows a failed test rather than trust after a passed one.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells Lucilius to consider for a long time whether to admit someone as a friend, but once he has decided, to welcome him wholeheartedly and speak as freely with him as with himself.
philosophy.explanation: Deliberation comes before friendship and full confidence after it.
philosophy.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s two commands almost exactly: do not trust without examination; after examination, trust.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; one of the closest parallels anywhere to this couplet’s structure.

kurals.tamil:
தேரான் தெளிவும் தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்
தீரா இடும்பை தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thaeraan thelivum thelindhaankan aiyuravum
Theeraa idumbai tharum.
kurals.meaning: Trusting someone you have not examined, and doubting someone you have examined and trusted, both bring endless trouble.
kurals.elementary: There are two ways to mess up with friends. One is trusting someone you just met with a big secret. The other is having a friend who has always been loyal and still checking their bag every day. Both make life miserable. Check carefully once, then trust.
kurals.university: The closing couplet names two opposite errors: தேரான் தெளிவு, confidence without examination (the fault of 508), and தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு, suspicion toward someone already tested and trusted. Both produce தீரா இடும்பை, ‘unending affliction’, repeating word for word the second line of 508, so the chapter ends by balancing its warnings: examination is required, but once done it must be honoured. Suspicion of a proven servant damages morale, invites real disloyalty, and wastes the effort of testing, points modern commentators such as Pappaiah and Kalaignar make explicit in the setting of appointments. The next chapter (52, தெரிந்து வினையாடல்) goes on to how the trusted person should be employed. Both sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After Sita has been rescued and her purity publicly confirmed by the fire ordeal, Rama later sends her into exile in response to gossip in Ayodhya, bringing lasting grief to both of them and to their family.
hinduism.explanation: Doubt revived after a trust has been proven leads to lasting sorrow.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s second error: suspicion toward one already tested and trusted.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 118 and Uttara Kanda 43-45
hinduism._accuracy_note: Tradition presents Rama as yielding to public opinion rather than doubting Sita himself, so the parallel is partial.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then saith he to Thomas, reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus rebukes Thomas for holding on to doubt despite the reliable testimony of the other disciples.
christianity.tie_back: Persisting in doubt when evidence already warrants trust is the error the Kural warns about.
christianity._accuracy_note: Only partly parallel: it concerns faith in the risen Christ, not trust in a tested person.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin.”
islam.explanation: Believers are told not to harbour baseless suspicion of one another or spy on each other.
islam.tie_back: Unfounded suspicion toward those already proven trustworthy is the Kural’s ஐயுறவு.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on the harm of suspicion; the verse is general rather than about appointees.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Joshua ben Perahiah used to say: appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah pairs choosing a companion with the duty to give people the benefit of the doubt.
judaism.tie_back: Choose carefully, then do not meet the chosen one with suspicion, which is the balance of the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on the second half; the warning against untested trust is not explicit here.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares a mind troubled by doubt (vicikicchā) to muddy water stirred up and set in the dark, in which a person cannot see their own reflection; doubt is one of the five hindrances.
buddhism.explanation: Persistent doubt keeps the mind from seeing clearly and acting well.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise treats needless doubt as a source of lasting affliction.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Only a partial parallel: vicikicchā is doubt about the path, not suspicion of a tested person.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Cephalus, doubting his faithful wife Procris, tests her in disguise; their marriage is later poisoned by mutual suspicion, and Procris, secretly following him out of jealousy, is killed by his own javelin.
greek_mythology.explanation: Suspicion toward a proven partner destroys what it was meant to protect.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Doubting the one already proven brings grief that cannot be undone, as the Kural warns.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A strong narrative match for the second error; the setting is marriage rather than office.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that only the friendship of good people is proof against slander, because it is not easy to believe anyone speaking against someone we have ourselves tested over a long time; among such friends there is trust and the thought ‘he would never wrong me’.
philosophy.explanation: Long testing produces a trust that should not be shaken by talk.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural too says that once someone is tested, doubting them is the error.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a close conceptual match to both halves (testing, then steady trust).
